name: MySQL
summary: The long-standing open-source SQL database behind much of the web, built on the InnoDB engine.
intro: MySQL is a client-server SQL database whose storage is handled by a pluggable engine; the default, and the one almost everyone uses, is InnoDB. InnoDB stores each table as a clustered index on its primary key, so rows sit in key order and a primary-key lookup goes straight to the data. It gives ACID transactions with row-level locking, and consistent reads through MVCC, so readers don’t wait for writers.

Replication is MySQL’s classic scaling tool. The primary records every change in its binary log, and replicas copy and replay it, which spreads read traffic across machines. Replication is asynchronous by default; semisynchronous mode makes a commit wait until at least one replica has the change, and GTIDs let replicas track position without log file offsets. Oracle ships two tracks: LTS series (8.4 and 9.7) that get only fixes for years, and Innovation releases with new features, each supported only until the next.
strengths: Mature, widely known, and offered as a managed service on every major cloud
Simple, well-understood replication for read scaling and failover
Primary-key lookups are fast because InnoDB stores rows in key order
LTS series change little, which keeps upgrades predictable
limits: With default asynchronous replication, a failover can lose the last commits that hadn’t reached a replica
Random primary keys such as UUIDv4 scatter inserts across the clustered index, which can leave its pages only half full
Innovation releases are supported only until the next one, so production usually stays on LTS
GPLv2: distributing it inside closed-source software needs a commercial licence from Oracle

story: Michael “Monty” Widenius and David Axmark wanted a SQL interface on top of their own fast, low-level ISAM table routines. They tried mSQL, a small database of the time, but found it neither fast enough nor flexible enough. So they wrote their own SQL layer, keeping almost the same API as mSQL so that code written for it could be ported easily. MySQL, named after Widenius’s daughter My, counts May 23, 1995 as its birthday, and with Allan Larsson they founded MySQL AB in Sweden to develop it.

MySQL AB released it under the GPL and sold commercial licences to companies that didn’t want the GPL’s terms. Fast, simple and free, it became the M in the LAMP stack (Linux, Apache, MySQL and PHP, Perl or Python), and by the end of 2004 the company claimed more than 5 million active installations. Its default engine, MyISAM, had no transactions; users who needed them could choose InnoDB, a transactional engine from the Finnish company Innobase.

Then ownership moved fast. Oracle bought Innobase in October 2005, Sun Microsystems agreed in January 2008 to buy MySQL AB for about $1 billion, and Oracle completed its purchase of Sun in January 2010. Worried about Oracle’s stewardship, Widenius forked MySQL as MariaDB, named after his second daughter, Maria. Oracle still develops MySQL today.

choices.why: MySQL began as a quick SQL front end for fast ISAM routines. Its early default engine, MyISAM, skipped transactions, so full ACID guarantees had to come from another engine.
Third-party code written for mSQL could be ported to MySQL easily.
The SQL layer is separate from how tables are stored, so a third party’s transactional engine, InnoDB, could slot in. It became the default in MySQL 5.5 in 2010.

choices.choice: GPL for everyone, a paid licence for the rest
choices.why: Dual licensing kept MySQL free under the GPL, while companies shipping it inside closed products bought commercial licences, one of MySQL AB’s three main sources of revenue.
